prompt: In Brooks's sense, what makes a piece of complexity "accidental"?
hint: Brooks took the word from philosophy, not from everyday speech.

choices.text: It was introduced by mistake or carelessness
choices.why: That is the everyday meaning, and the misreading the lesson warns about. Accidental complexity is often the result of a sensible decision.

choices.text: Another decision could have solved the same problem without it
choices.why: Right: it belongs to how the system was built, not to the problem, so a different way of building could have avoided it.

choices.text: Nobody decided to add it; it appeared over time
choices.why: Most of Carreto's accidental complexity was decided on purpose, each piece for a reason on the day.

choices.text: It lives in the infrastructure rather than in the business code
choices.why: Business code holds plenty of accidental complexity too, such as a status kept in two places. The line is essence against accident, not code against servers.

prompt: Which of these is essential complexity at Carreto?
hint: Would it remain whatever architecture Carreto chose?

choices.text: Keeping a load's status in two places, synced every night
choices.why: A copy Carreto chose to make for its search service; another design would not need it.

choices.text: Three different ways of configuring a service
choices.why: Pure accident: no freight, tax or money rule asks for three.

choices.text: Applying the ANTT floor to every quote
choices.why: Right: the minimum freight floor is law. Any design has to know it and apply it; a design expresses it more or less clearly, and that is all.

choices.text: Calling geo-distance over HTTP from matching
choices.why: The distance calculation is needed; doing it over a network hop was a choice, later reversed.

prompt: Paula measured about 6 hours of routine upgrade work per service per month. How many hours a month is that across Carreto's 14 services?
hint: Hours per service times services.

prompt: A small service took 120 hours to build and costs 10 hours a month to keep. After how many months has keeping it cost as much as building it?
hint: Divide the one-off cost by the monthly one.

prompt: An architect tells the board she will "cut the complexity of CT-e issuance in half" next year. What is wrong with the promise, by the lesson?
hint: Whose complexity is most of it?

choices.text: CT-e issuance is already as simple as it gets
choices.why: Carreto's CT-e code may well carry accidental complexity worth removing. The problem is the size of the promise, not that nothing is left.

choices.text: Halving it needs a rewrite, which the tech-strategy course rules out
choices.why: Neither this lesson nor that course makes such a rule, and a rewrite would not shrink the tax authority's rules.

choices.text: Most of it is the tax authority's; a design expresses it, it does not remove it
choices.why: Right: the layout, the validation and the rejections are essential complexity. Promising to halve them is promising to simplify the tax authority.

choices.text: Simplifying is a decision for the team, not something an architect promises
choices.why: An architect may well argue for simplification, as Renata did. The flaw is in what this particular promise claims.

prompt: Which of these does a deployable service cost every month, even when nobody changes its code? Choose all that apply.
hint: One option is paid once.

choices.text: A place on the on-call rota, with a runbook
choices.why: Yes: somebody carries its pager whether or not it changes.

choices.text: Upgrades to its libraries, framework and base image
choices.why: Yes: they age on their own schedule, about 6 hours a month per service at Carreto.

choices.text: The engineering time to write it in the first place
choices.why: That is the building cost, paid once. The lesson's point is that the keeping cost is larger and has no bill.

choices.text: Somebody who remembers why it exists and what calls it
choices.why: Yes: knowledge is a cost, and it leaves with the person unless the service leaves first.

prompt: What pattern did Renata find in the five services she proposed removing?
hint: Look at the "what calls it" column.

choices.text: They were the five oldest services at Carreto
choices.why: Age was not the test. Tracking is old and kept its place.

choices.text: Each had one caller, or none that needed it
choices.why: Right: a service with one caller has none of the benefits a service exists for, and every one of its costs.

choices.text: All five belonged to the Platform team
choices.why: They belonged to Pricing, Payments, Matching and Platform.

choices.text: They raised the most pages of the fourteen
choices.why: Together they raised 29 of the 112 pages: real, but not the pattern that identified them.

prompt: Why did load-search go to Helena instead of being removed by engineering like the other four?
hint: What does a shipper lose when it goes?

choices.text: It was the most expensive of the five to take away
choices.why: Cost was not the issue; the lesson gives no such comparison.

choices.text: The Matching team refused to give up its own service
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says Matching objected.

choices.text: Taking it away removes a feature, which is a product decision
choices.why: Right: 4% of shippers use its search screen. Whether that feature stays is Helena's call, not the architect's.

choices.text: Its search cluster holds the only copy of the open loads
choices.why: The monolith's table is the original; load-search keeps a copy, synced nightly.

prompt: Put the steps for removing a service safely in the lesson's order.
hint: Evidence first, deletion last.
items: Find every caller from the traffic
Move the callers, one small change at a time
Watch the old service receive nothing for two weeks
Switch it off and keep it switchable for a month
Delete the pipeline, alerts, dashboards, secrets and documents
trap: Deleting before the quiet period is how a fortnightly job nobody remembered discovers the service is gone.

prompt: A team wants to switch off an old reporting service today because the wiki lists no callers. What should come first, by the lesson?
hint: Which source says who calls a service now?

choices.text: Check the access logs and the broker's consumers for callers
choices.why: Right: traffic says who calls it now; the wiki says who called it when the page was written.

choices.text: Ask the original author, who will know what still depends on it
choices.why: Worth a message, but memory is the same kind of evidence as the wiki. The lesson starts from traffic.

choices.text: Switch it off on a Friday and see who complains
choices.why: That discovers callers by breaking them, and the weekend makes the breakage last longer.

choices.text: Update the wiki first, so the removal is documented
choices.why: Documentation comes at the end, once the service is gone; here it would record a guess.

prompt: Why does removal need the architect, instead of waiting for a team to do it?
hint: Look at who pays and who saves.

choices.text: Only the architect has the access needed to delete services
choices.why: Teams delete their own services; access is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Removal is risky, and the architect answers for structural risk
choices.why: The risk is handled by the safe-removal steps. The obstacle the lesson names is about incentives.

choices.text: Teams rarely notice what their own services cost
choices.why: Pricing knew what pricing-floor cost it. The point is where the cost and the saving land.

choices.text: The cost falls on one team while the saving spreads across all
choices.why: Right: no team's roadmap will carry work whose benefit goes to everybody else. The architect sees the whole inventory and argues for the time.

prompt: Carreto removed four services, each with about 6 hours a month of upgrade work. How many hours of upgrade work does that save in a year?
hint: Services, times hours a month, times months.

prompt: In Hickey's terms, what separates simple from easy?
hint: One is a property of the thing; the other depends on who is looking.

choices.text: Simple is fewer lines of code; easy is fewer services
choices.why: Neither is a count. A short function can braid three concerns together.

choices.text: Simple is tangling; easy is nearness to us
choices.why: Right: simple means not intertwined with other things and is the same for everybody; easy means familiar and close at hand, and depends on the person.

choices.text: Simple is what juniors understand; easy is what seniors prefer
choices.why: That makes both relative to people. Hickey's point is that only one of them is.

choices.text: They mean the same, and the talk was about style
choices.why: The talk exists to pull them apart, because confusing them leads to the easy choice that tangles a system.

prompt: Payments learnt about proved deliveries by reading Tracking's tables directly. Where does that choice sit on Hickey's two axes?
hint: It worked on the first day. What happened six months later?

choices.text: Simple and easy
choices.why: Easy, yes: the database was right there. But it braided two teams together through one table.

choices.text: Simple, and hard at first
choices.why: That describes the interface Tracking owns, which took a week.

choices.text: Easy, and complex
choices.why: Right: close at hand on the day, and tangled from then on. Tracking could not rename a column without breaking Payments.

choices.text: Complex, and hard to build
choices.why: It was not hard at all; that is exactly why it was chosen.

prompt: Hickey revived an old English verb for braiding things together, which is how systems get complicated: to ___.
hint: The verb behind the word "complex".

prompt: A team proposes moving invoicing out of the monolith into a new service that keeps reading and writing the monolith's database, and deploys together with it. Is that a simplification?
hint: Count the braids, not the boxes.

choices.text: Yes: each service now owns a smaller share of the code
choices.why: Size per box is not the measure. The two still share data and a release.

choices.text: Yes, if it gets its own on-call rota
choices.why: A rota adds a cost; it does not untangle anything.

choices.text: No, because a monolith is simpler than any set of services
choices.why: Too strong: services that each own one concept and their own data untangle things. This proposal does not.

choices.text: No: a box was added and the braid kept, a distributed monolith
choices.why: Right: shared tables and joint deploys keep the tangle and add every monthly cost of a service, with none of the independence.

prompt: What does an "innovation token", in Dan McKinley's essay, stand for?
hint: Each company gets about three.

choices.text: A chance to use technology new to the company
choices.why: Right: every new database, language or platform spends one, so spend them where the company is trying to be different.

choices.text: A budget line for experiments, renewed every year
choices.why: The tokens are not money and are not renewed; they stand for the company's limited capacity to operate unfamiliar technology.

choices.text: A reward a team earns by shipping on time
choices.why: Nothing is earned. The point is a limit on how much novelty a company can carry.

choices.text: A vote each team has at the architecture forum
choices.why: The forum is lesson 10's; the tokens are about technology choices, not voting.

prompt: Which part of Carreto's history fits John Gall's law?
hint: A complex system that works grew from what?

choices.text: pricing-floor, designed in advance for business users who never came
choices.why: That is the counter-example: something designed ahead for a load that never arrived.

choices.text: Tracking, cut out of a working monolith when a real load demanded it
choices.why: Right: the monolith worked first, and the service earned its place when the GPS volume required it.

choices.text: The fourteen services, planned together as one system in the first year
choices.why: Nobody planned fourteen; each was added on its own day.

choices.text: The config-service, which replaced environment variables everywhere
choices.why: It never replaced them; it became a third way to configure things, and was deleted.

prompt: The Matching team proposes a graph database to choose candidate drivers. Which response fits the lesson?
hint: Neither a yes nor a no.

choices.text: Ask what it buys that PostgreSQL does not, and try PostgreSQL first
choices.why: Right: the PostgreSQL version met the target in a week, and the token stayed unspent.

choices.text: Refuse: Carreto's tokens are already spent
choices.why: Renata did not refuse. A token may be worth spending; the team has to show it.

choices.text: Approve it: matching is where Carreto is different from others
choices.why: It might be a good place for a token, but approving before asking what it buys skips the argument.

choices.text: Ask Platform to run it, so Matching carries no extra on-call
choices.why: That moves the cost to another team without asking whether it is worth paying.

prompt: Match each work to the idea this lesson took from it.
hint: Brooks, Hickey, McKinley and Gall.

pairs.right: simple is not the same as easy
working complex systems grow from simple ones

prompt: A team cites YAGNI as the reason to skip tests on a new Pricing module. What does the lesson say?
hint: Fowler marks where the rule stops.

choices.text: Fair: tests are a capability nobody has asked for yet
choices.why: Tests are not a feature for a presumed need; they are what keeps the code cheap to change.

choices.text: Fair, if the module is small enough to rewrite later
choices.why: Size does not change the argument; a small module without tests is still slower to change safely.

choices.text: YAGNI is from the 1990s and no longer applies to services
choices.why: The lesson applies it to services directly: pricing-floor was a presumptive feature.

choices.text: YAGNI covers presumed features, not tests
choices.why: Right: tests, refactoring and clear boundaries make it cheap to add the feature when it is really needed. Cutting them defeats the rule's purpose.

prompt: pricing-floor was split out so business people could change the floor without a deploy, and they never did. Of Fowler's four costs of a presumptive feature, which one did every quote pay?
hint: A cost paid for as long as the thing exists.

choices.text: The cost of building it
choices.why: Paid once, in 2020.

choices.text: The cost of delay
choices.why: The work not done while it was built; also paid once.

choices.text: The cost of repairing it
choices.why: Repair applies when the presumed need turns out different and the feature has to be reworked.

choices.text: The cost of carrying it
choices.why: Right: the cost of carry, paid on every quote. Each one made a network call to it, and twice its outage stopped Pricing quoting at all.
